title: How Did Yang Guifei's Lychees Reach Chang'an?
description:
Late-Tang poet Du Mu wrote "A rider in red dust, the consort smiles; no one knows the lychees have come," and the Song-compiled New Book of Tang says the lychees "ran thousands of li and reached the capital, their taste unchanged." Yet Tang writer Li Zhao says lychees "spoil overnight," and Bai Juyi that off the branch "in three days the taste changes." This episode follows the records in the order they were written. Relay stations stood every 30 li, and an edict of the 7th month of Tianbao 5 made exiled officials "ride ten stations a day." On where the fruit came from, Tang writers give Du Fu's "envoy from Nanhai," Li Zhao's "those grown in Nanhai beat Shu's," and the Zizhi Tongjian's "ordered yearly from Lingnan." In the Song, Cai Xiang and Su Dongpo name Fuzhou in Sichuan; Wu Zeng first calls Lingnan "clear," then changes his mind; Southern Song gazetteers add the Consort's Orchard and "seven days and nights." Chen Zhengmin and Wang Guanguo say Du Mu got the season wrong, Cheng Dachang defends him, and the Old Book of Tang records one visit to Huaqing Palace in summer, 4th month, Tianbao 8. Relay horses carrying lychees, and the Song quarrel over the poem: on file. Where they came from, how many days, how fresh on arrival: still open.

Classical texts: Daizhige v2.0 transcriptions and Wikisource; the Yudi Jisheng from National Library of China manuscript images. Distances stay in li, as in the sources. "Seven days and nights" is a Song gazetteer's claim, not a Tang record.

Illustrations are AI-generated; historical figures are unnamed cartoon characters.

Information as of 2026-10-20

lz101.text: In Tianbao 15, Yang Guifei died on the road as the court fled.

lz102.text: Decades on, late-Tang poet Du Mu wrote of Mount Li's Huaqing Palace:

lz103.text: A rider's dust, the consort smiles; none know it's lychees.

lz104.text: The Song-era New Book of Tang: lychees ran thousands of li and reached the capital still fresh.

lz105.text: But Bai Juyi wrote: three days off the branch, and the taste has changed.

lz106.text: In Tianbao 5, an edict set the stations to cover a day;

lz107.text: Du Fu wrote of an envoy racing to present lychees. Where was he from?

lz108.text: One Song scholar wrote about it twice, in the same book;

lz109.text: And some in the Song said Du Mu's poem didn't fit the facts.

lz110.text: So how did Yang Guifei's lychees reach Chang'an?

lz201.text: The answer is just before that New Book of Tang line: "riders set to relay it," station to station.

lz202.text: A Tang station every 30 li or so; over 1,600 in all.

lz203.text: How many could a rider cover a day?

lz204.text: The rule: routine business, at most four a day.

lz205.text: For urgent ones, the pass gave the stations per day;

lz207.text: That opening edict came in the 7th month of Tianbao 5:

lz208.text: Exiled officials dawdled; now graver offenders had to make ten stations or more a day.

lz210.text: The Zizhi Tongjian sets this edict by the lychees,

lz211.text: and adds: from then on, many exiles never arrived alive.

lz212.text: And how many days could lychees last?

lz213.text: In Tang Guoshi Bu, Tang writer Li Zhao says lychees ripen in midsummer and spoil overnight.

lz214.text: Bai Juyi spelled out those three days:

lz215.text: Off the branch, color turns in a day, scent in two; in four or five days, it's all gone.

lz216.text: As an official in Zhongzhou, east Sichuan, he had a lychee painted. For whom?

lz217.text: Those who never saw them fresh.

lz218.text: Had officials in Chang'an seen one?

lz219.text: In the Kaiyuan years, Zhang Jiuling, from Lingnan, praised lychees in Chang'an;

lz220.text: Most peers neither knew nor believed.

lz221.text: Bai Juyi, an official in Chang'an for years, first picked one in Zhongzhou.

lz222.text: So where did the lychees rushed to Chang'an start out?

lz301.text: Tang poet Du Fu says: Nanhai, the far south. In Shangyuan 2, his poem recalls that envoy:

lz302.text: Remembering how, back then, an envoy from Nanhai raced in with lychees.

lz303.text: Of Tang poems in this file, it's nearest to Tianbao and names Nanhai.

lz304.text: Years later he wrote: after Xuanzong and the consort died, lychees still went to Chang'an.

lz305.text: Another Tang poet, Bao Fang, went further:

lz306.text: 5th month, ripe lychees leave Xiang at dawn, reach Hangu Pass by dusk.

lz307.text: We think it's poetry, not a speed record.

lz308.text: So how far was Lingnan from Chang'an?

lz309.text: Tang gazetteers put Lingnan's Guangzhou from Chang'an at over 4,200 li; another road, over 5,000.

lz310.text: Remember Li Zhao's "spoil overnight"? The same note begins:

lz311.text: The consort, born in Shu, loved lychees; Nanhai's beat Shu's, so they were rushed in every year.

lz312.text: So Shu had lychees too. Keep that word in mind: Shu.

lz313.text: The late-Tang tale Ganze Yao has a scene on Mount Li:

lz314.text: On her birthday, Xuanzong hears a new tune at Changsheng Hall; Nanhai lychees come,

lz316.text: Then in the Song, Sima Guang's Zizhi Tongjian is blunt:

lz317.text: Ordered yearly from Lingnan, by relay.

lz318.text: Only this history we opened names Lingnan;

lz319.text: but it came two or three centuries after Tianbao.

lz320.text: Yet also in the Song, someone named another place. Which one?

lz401.text: Fuzhou, in Sichuan. Northern Song writer Cai Xiang, in Lizhi Pu:

lz402.text: In Tianbao, the Tang consort adored them; Fuzhou sent them yearly by relay.

lz403.text: The earliest naming Fuzhou that we found;

lz404.text: He adds: however fast, little color, scent or taste survived.

lz405.text: Li Zhao's "Shu" is back: Fuzhou lies in Sichuan.

lz406.text: Su Dongpo, in a note to a poem, agreed:

lz407.text: In Tianbao, likely Fuzhou's, via Ziwu Valley into Chang'an.

lz409.text: Tang gazetteers: Fuzhou to Chang'an, 2,200 to over 2,300 li,

lz411.text: Bai Juyi's Zhongzhou? Next door, downriver from Fuzhou;

lz412.text: Did its lychees reach the capital?

lz413.text: No. He wrote: these can't be tribute; they never reach the capital.

lz414.text: That was Bai's time, though; it can't rule out Tianbao.

lz415.text: The Song scholar who wrote about it twice was Wu Zeng.

lz416.text: First: histories and Du Fu point south; Xuanzong's lychees clearly came from Lingnan.

lz417.text: Yet later in the same book, he changed his mind.

lz418.text: He read a Fuzhou Tujing and asked locals:

lz419.text: Fuzhou had a Consort's Orchard; a shortcut to Chang'an took under seven days.

lz420.text: Su Dongpo was from Sichuan too, he said, so he knew.

lz421.text: We think his change rested on gazetteers and locals' word, not Tang documents.

lz422.text: How was that orchard written up later?

lz423.text: Southern Song gazetteer Yudi Jisheng lists it among Fuzhou's relics:

lz424.text: Relay horses reached the capital in seven days and nights; men and horses died in droves.

lz425.text: Remember Du Mu's opening poem? The gazetteer copies it into the orchard entry, saying: this is the place.

lz426.text: Copying it later, the Fangyu Shenglan prefixed four characters: "as the Tujing tells."

lz427.text: At the Song's seven days and nights, how many li a day?

lz428.text: Over 300, about the pace the Tianbao 5 edict forced on exiles.

lz432.text: Even the gazetteer says Fuzhou's are famous only for the consort, lesser than Luzhou's or Xuzhou's.

lz433.text: And the Song critic who faulted Du Mu: what did he pick on?

lz501.text: The month. Around Chongning and Daguan, Northern Song writer Chen Zhengmin wrote:

lz502.text: Xuanzong went to Mount Li each 10th month, back by spring, never there in the 6th; recall Li Zhao? Lychees ripen in midsummer.

lz503.text: His verdict: a fine line, but not the facts.

lz504.text: Another Song man, Wang Guanguo: by the time they arrived, she'd long left Huaqing Palace.

lz505.text: But someone defended Du Mu: Cheng Dachang.

lz506.text: Remember the Ganze Yao scene on Mount Li? Cheng dug out its date:

lz507.text: Tianbao 14, 6th month, 1st day: her birthday, with Xuanzong on Mount Li.

lz508.text: He cites a notebook: each 7th night of the 7th month, the pair feasted at Huaqing;

lz509.text: and Bai Juyi's Everlasting Sorrow: 7th of the 7th, Changsheng Hall.

lz510.text: Du Mu, he said, wrote what was truly handed down.

lz511.text: But we think he cites a tale, notes and poems, not histories.

lz513.text: The histories record dozens of trips to Mount Li, most as Chen Zhengmin said.

lz514.text: But the Old Book of Tang's annals, for summer, Tianbao 8, 4th month, say:

lz515.text: To Huaqing's Guanfeng Tower. That's all; no word on how long;

lz516.text: The New Book of Tang's annals and Zizhi Tongjian omit it.

lz517.text: Du Mu's own long poem sets Huaqing in the 8th month: "towers cool in month 8."

lz518.text: Remember the rider in red dust? In the same long poem, ruined Huaqing Palace holds only scattered lychee baskets.

lz519.text: Relay horses with lychees, Song scholars feuding over the poem: on file. Where from, how many days, how fresh on arrival: still open.

lz520.text: Do you think Du Mu's red-dust rider got the season wrong?

lz521.text: We tell only what records show. Subscribe to open the files with us.
